newsitem.title: USA: U.S. slaps sanctions against Japanese ships.
newsitem.headline: U.S. slaps sanctions against Japanese ships.

text.p: The U.S. Maritime Commission hit Japanese shipping companies with $100,000 port surcharges Wednesday in response to what it said were "unfavorable restrictive practices" at Japanese ports.
The commission said it decided to put the surcharge into effect April 14 after it found that repeated diplomatic efforts over the last several years failed to bring about necessary reforms.

The Japan Harbour Transportation Association (JHTA), an association of Japanese waterfront employees, has put in place costly and restrictive practices that discriminate against foreign vessels, the commission said.

Shippers are not allowed to make operational changes, major or minor, without the permission of the JHTA, the commission said. The JHTA exercises its control through a "prior consultation" system of negotiations and pre-approvals involving carriers, JHTA and waterfront unions, it said.

The commission said there was no way to appeal JHTA decisions and that it "uses its control over access to the prior consultation system to suppress competition and allocate work among its member companies.

"The commission also found that JHTA uses its authority to disrupt the business operations of its detractors, extract payment of unwarranted fees, and impose operational restrictions, such as Sunday work limits," it said.

The commission said the surcharge will be imposed each time a vessel owned or operated by Kawasaki Kisen Kaisha Ltd., Mitsui O.S.K. Lines Ltd. and Nippon Yusen KK enters a U.S. port from abroad, but not from another U.S. port.
"The fee represents a measured approach to Japanese port conditions, crafted to respond firmly to Japanese practices without disrupting U.S. trade and ocean commerce," the commission said.

"While a commercially significant amount, the fee represents only a small percentage of Japanese carriers' total per-voyage revenues, and is unlikely to result in adverse effects for U.S. ports and shippers," the commission said.
The commission also said it found that Japan's licensing requirements for terminal operators and stevedoring companies also discriminate against foreign firms.
The commission said that if Japan moves to retaliate against U.S. lines, the level of fees on Japanese carriers would be increased proportionally.

The European Union has also complained about Japanese port practices. Japanese shipping companies have argued that the U.S. commission's charges were not based on facts and that they do not decide port practices.
